The Couma sea catfish (Sciades couma) exhibits a maximum recorded total length of 97 centimeters [Li = 97 centimeters], a size that positions it among the larger members of the Ariidae family in neotropical estuaries. Analyses of length-at-age data from populations in the Amazon delta indicate that females attain puberty at a total length of 36.6 cm [Lp = 36.6 cm], though standard length measurements from earlier studies have reported values near 51 cm. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae, emerging after the egg stage typically found in demersal, adhesive egg masses guarded by the male, display a wet weight at birth of 2.14 grams [Wwb = 2.14 grams]. This modest initial mass reflects the relatively small size of the fertilised ova, and the rapid transition to exogenous feeding that characterises the early larval phase in ariid catfishes. The species is known to reach a maximum recorded age of 5 years [am = 5 years] under natural conditions, a lifespan that is intermediate for catfishes of comparable body size inhabiting seasonal tropical systems at a temperature of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C]. This longevity, combined with its substantial asymptotic size, suggests a life history strategy that balances moderate parental investment in large, yolk-rich eggs against the frequent reproductive events necessary to exploit productive but ephemeral floodplain habitats.

Reproductive output in Sciades couma has been quantified under controlled thermal conditions. At a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], females produce approximately 165 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 165 eggs per year], reflecting the production of large, nutrient-dense ova that require extended incubation within the male's buccal cavity—a characteristic reproductive mode of the Ariidae. The wet weight at puberty, calculated from the length-weight relationship for this species, is 588 grams [Wwp = 588 grams], indicating that females must accumulate considerable somatic reserves before initiating vitellogenesis and the onset of gonadal recrudescence. This threshold weight is attained only after several years of growth, consistent with the length at first sexual maturation reported in field surveys. The interplay between a relatively high annual egg production and a large pubertal mass suggests that reproductive allocation becomes significant only after a prolonged period of somatic investment, a pattern observed in other iteroparous, nest-guarding ariids from the Amazon and Orinoco basins.

Field studies and laboratory rearing experiments have provided detailed insights into the growth trajectory and maximal body dimensions of Sciades couma. The ultimate wet weight, derived from its asymptotic total length, reaches 12,500 grams [Wwi = 12,500 grams], making it one of the more massive catfish species in its range. This impressive adult body mass is supported by a diet dominated by benthic invertebrates and small fishes, which the adults forage for over expansive mudflats and river channels. In contrast, the mass at birth of 2.14 grams [Wwb = 2.14 grams] represents only a tiny fraction of this ultimate size, underscoring the dramatic growth multiple required to achieve reproductive maturity. The total length at puberty of 36.6 cm [Lp = 36.6 cm] corresponds to roughly 38 percent of the ultimate total length of 97 cm [Li = 97 cm], a proportional size at maturation that is typical for many slow-growing, large-bodied estuarine teleosts. This growth pattern implies that individuals allocate most of their early energetic budget to somatic expansion, delaying reproduction until they have reached a size capable of producing competitively viable egg masses.

Longevity data for wild populations of Sciades couma indicate that the maximum lifespan is approximately 1,825 days [am = approximately 1,825 days] when assessed at an ambient water temperature of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C]. This age corresponds to the oldest individuals captured in mark-recapture studies conducted in the lower Amazon estuary, where thermal regimes are relatively stable year-round. The lifespan of 5 years [am = 5 years] is consistent with that predicted by life-history theory for a fish of its asymptotic mass, although some congeneric species in cooler, less productive waters may live longer at a temperature of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C]. The combination of a moderate lifespan and a protracted growth period suggests that senescence in this species is gradual, with reproductive performance potentially declining only in the final year of life.

The morphological and physiological constraints acting on Sciades couma are reflected in the scaling relationships between body size and reproductive investment. The wet weight at puberty of 588 grams [Wwp = 588 grams] represents approximately 4.7 percent of the ultimate wet weight of 12,500 grams [Wwi = 12,500 grams], a ratio that indicates a relatively late onset of reproduction compared to many other ariid species. In contrast, the neonatal wet weight of 2.14 grams [Wwb = 2.14 grams] is roughly 0.017 percent of the asymptotic body mass, a value that aligns with the production of moderately large, yolk-rich eggs that are typical of mouthbrooding catfishes. Under the thermal conditions typical of their native range, where water temperatures average 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C], the total length of 36.6 cm [Lp = 36.6 cm] at puberty is achieved after several years of sustained growth. The ultimate total length of 97 cm [Li = 97 cm] is rarely attained, with most individuals in heavily fished areas reaching only 70 to 80 cm, highlighting the impact of selective exploitation on the demographic structure of this species.
